Designing useful underwater thrust

The thruster needed a geometry the team could fabricate, integrate, and test.

As mechanical design lead, I developed the ducted propeller and thruster assembly in SolidWorks, studied the flow using Flow Simulation, and worked with the electrical team on prototype integration. I also helped teammates understand the CFD setup, assembly, and testing process.

Use flow analysis to inform the geometry

I used the duct and rotating-region model to examine the flow around the propeller and compare the design choices. Velocity trajectories made it easier to discuss what the duct was doing and where a revision might be useful.

Connect thrust and mass flow
T ≈ ṁ(vout − vin)

This simplified momentum relationship helps interpret propeller flow. It neglects pressure and other control-volume terms; full performance depends on the geometry, speed, flow conditions, and test setup.

Prototype and team integration

The project moved from CAD and CFD into fabricated prototypes and testing. Prototype testing produced approximately 10 N of thrust under the project’s test conditions.

The work also involved explaining manufacturing and installation considerations to teammates, aligning mechanical interfaces with the electrical system, and making the assembly testable.

What I learned

PROJECT STATUS

CAD and CFD supported a tested prototype.

This project gave me experience connecting a fluid-mechanics model with fabrication and team integration. It also reinforced the need to compare analysis with measurements before making a performance claim.
